title: Effective Field Theory for a Baryon-Correlated Dark Matter Profile
comment: 19 pages. Companion paper to "Resolving the Core-Cusp and Diversity Problems with a Baryon-Correlated Dark Matter Profile"
summary: While the standard $Λ$CDM model succeeds on large cosmological scales, it faces persistent small-scale challenges, including the core-cusp problem, the diversity of galaxy rotation curves, and the Tully-Fisher relation. To address these issues, we recently proposed an empirical law where the effective dark matter energy density is directly correlated with the baryonic gravitational potential, $ρ_{\rm DM} \propto Φ_b^2$, which reproduces observed rotation curves and resolves the core-cusp and diversity problems. To provide a theoretical foundation for this empirical law, we construct an effective field theory (EFT) introducing massive scalar, vector, and tensor mediators between baryons and a dark sector field $χ$. We demonstrate that aligning the mediator couplings to a specific ratio (4:6:3) with degenerate masses exactly cancels the additional fifth forces acting on baryons up to $O(v^2)$. We then show that this theoretical framework originates from a 5-dimensional (5D) spacetime. Treating the baryonic source as a 5D null fluid reveals that the three mediators emerge from a single 5D symmetric tensor field. By confining the field $χ$ to a 4D brane, we reveal that its interaction with these mediators generates a pressureless energy density ($ρ_{\rm int} \propto Φ_b^2$) that yields the empirically required baryon-correlated profile. Consequently, the field $χ$ exhibits a scale-dependent transition: on cosmological scales, its mass energy acts as standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM), whereas on galactic scales, its interaction energy governs local dynamics. Finally, by evaluating the dynamical boundary of this localized interaction region, we provide a physical interpretation that yields the relation $μ= K M_b^{-3/2}$, offering a theoretical basis for the Tully-Fisher relation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an effective field theory where massive scalar, vector, and tensor mediators (with 4:6:3 coupling ratios) connect baryons to a dark sector field χ, derived from a 5D spacetime framework. The interaction energy (ρ_int ∝ Φ_b²) resolves the core-cusp and diversity problems, while the field χ transitions from CDM-like behavior on cosmological scales to baryon-correlated dynamics on galactic scales, with the Tully-Fisher relation (μ ∝ M_b^{-3/2}) emerging from the dynamical boundary of the interaction region.
AI.motivation: Standard ΛCDM faces small-scale challenges (core-cusp, rotation curve diversity, Tully-Fisher relation). The authors previously proposed an empirical law (ρ_DM ∝ Φ_b²) that resolves these issues, and now seek a theoretical foundation for it.
AI.method: Construct an EFT with massive scalar, vector, and tensor mediators between baryons and a dark field χ; require 4:6:3 coupling ratios and degenerate masses to cancel fifth forces up to O(v²). Embed the framework in 5D spacetime where the three mediators originate from a single 5D symmetric tensor field, with χ confined to a 4D brane.
AI.result: The interaction energy density ρ_int ∝ Φ_b² reproduces the baryon-correlated profile needed for the empirical law. The field χ transitions from CDM-like (mass energy dominant) on cosmological scales to interaction-energy-dominated on galactic scales. The Tully-Fisher relation μ ∝ M_b^{-3/2} emerges from the dynamical boundary of the localized interaction region.
AI.conclusion: A theoretical foundation from 5D spacetime naturally produces the empirical baryon-correlated dark matter profile, resolving small-scale ΛCDM anomalies and providing a physical basis for the Tully-Fisher relation.

title: Cosmological perturbations with $f(R)$ gravity scalarons : Galaxy power spectra and the scalaron mass
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
summary: In this paper we study cosmological perturbations with $f(R)$ gravity scalaron. We consider epoch of transition from early general relativity (GR) phase to late time non-GR phase of cosmogenic history for a viable $f(R)$ gravity Lagrangian close to the $Λ$CDM theory at early cosmic history. We study deviation in matter power spectra from $Λ$CDM scenario. Galaxy power spectra multipoles are generated using galaxy bias, velocity dispersion and modified gravity parameters. While monopole and quadrupole matter power in $f(R)$ theory increase towards larger $k$ (small scales), quadrupole power spectrum remains elevated relative to $Λ$CDM for smaller $k$ (large scales), upto $k\approx 0.02$. These power spectra provide observables for testing gravity through the current and future galaxy survey missions such as DESI, EUCLID, 4MOST and PFS. We report appropriate GR limit of scalaron mass in galactic and massive black hole scales. Evolution of the scalaron mass and its general relativistic limit for various cosmic structures are reported. Deviation from GR in cosmogenic evolution is attributed to decrease in scalaron mass with cosmic time.

AI.tldr: This paper studies cosmological perturbations in f(R) gravity, focusing on the transition from early GR to late non-GR phases. It analyzes matter power spectra deviations from ΛCDM, finding increased monopole and quadrupole power at small scales and elevated quadrupole at large scales (k≈0.02). The study reports GR limits of scalaron mass for galactic and black hole scales, and attributes GR deviation to decreasing scalaron mass over cosmic time.
AI.motivation: To understand deviations from ΛCDM in f(R) gravity theories by studying cosmological perturbations and matter power spectra, particularly the transition from early GR phase to late-time non-GR phase.
AI.method: The authors study cosmological perturbations with f(R) gravity scalaron, analyze matter power spectra deviations using galaxy bias, velocity dispersion, and modified gravity parameters, and generate galaxy power spectra multipoles (monopole and quadrupole).
AI.result: Monopole and quadrupole matter power in f(R) theory increase towards larger k (small scales). Quadrupole power remains elevated relative to ΛCDM for smaller k (large scales) up to k≈0.02. Deviation from GR is attributed to decreasing scalaron mass with cosmic time.
AI.conclusion: The power spectra provide observables for testing gravity through current/future surveys (DESI, EUCLID, 4MOST, PFS). The GR limit of scalaron mass is reported for galactic and massive black hole scales.

title: CMB Acoustic Power Spectra in STVG-MOG
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure
summary: We present a cosmological realization of Scalar--Tensor--Vector Gravity (STVG--MOG) in which the pre-recombination scalar perturbation dynamics become degenerate with those of $Λ$CDM without invoking particle dark matter. In the early universe, nonrelativistic excitations of the massive STVG vector field $φ_μ$ behave as a collisionless, pressureless component with vanishing sound speed and background density $ρ_φ\propto a^{-3}$. On the Fourier scales relevant for the acoustic peaks, the effective gravitational coupling satisfies $G_{\rm eff}(k,a)\simeq G_N$, so that the metric potentials governing baryon--photon oscillations evolve in the same way as in the standard cosmological model. The gravitational wells remain sufficiently deep at horizon entry to preserve the observed height of the third acoustic peak, the most sensitive indicator of a clustering pressureless component prior to recombination. Since Thomson scattering, recombination, baryon loading, and photon diffusion are unchanged, the temperature and polarization spectra can coincide with the standard $Λ$CDM predictions once the vector sector supplies the effective dust component. In this framework, the dynamical role usually attributed to cold dark matter is carried instead by a degree of freedom belonging to the gravitational sector itself. We explain why this vector-sector dust, although dynamically degenerate with cold dark matter in the early universe, is not equivalent to a particle dark matter fluid. The Boltzmann code CLASS is used to obtain a MOG fit to the acoustical power spectrum data.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that STVG-MOG theory can mimic ΛCDM's pre-recombination perturbation dynamics without particle dark matter, using a massive vector field that behaves like collisionless dust but belongs to the gravitational sector.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that a modified gravity theory (STVG-MOG) can reproduce ΛCDM cosmological perturbation behavior without invoking particle dark matter, specifically addressing the acoustic peak structure.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of scalar perturbation dynamics in STVG-MOG, showing that the vector field φ_μ yields a pressureless component with ρ_φ ∝ a^{-3}, vanishing sound speed, and G_eff(k,a) ≈ G_N on CMB scales; verification using the Boltzmann code CLASS.
AI.result: The vector field provides an effective dust component that preserves the third acoustic peak height and yields temperature/polarization spectra coincident with ΛCDM, as the metric potentials governing baryon-photon oscillations evolve identically to the standard model.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical role of cold dark matter can be carried by a gravitational-sector degree of freedom (the STVG vector field), which is not equivalent to particle dark matter despite being dynamically degenerate in the early universe.

title: The Splashback Mass Function of Galaxy Clusters from Photometric Data
comment: 19 pages, 17 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The splashback radius marks the physical boundary of galaxy clusters, separating orbiting from infalling material, and provides a halo definition free from pseudo-evolution. In this work, we present a fully photometric framework to measure individual cluster splashback radii and masses, and to construct an observational splashback mass function. Using Sloan Digital Sky Survey data, we develop a probabilistic cluster membership method based on radial and photometric redshift information, optimized through an adaptive probability cut that maximizes the detection significance of the cluster core relative to its outskirts. We apply this methodology to a sample of 499 galaxy clusters from the \textsc{CoMaLit} weak-lensing compilation and recover splashback radii from modeling cumulative galaxy number profiles. The resulting splashback radii exhibit a median ratio $R_{\mathrm{sp}}/R_{200\mathrm{m}} \simeq 1.1$, consistent with previous observational studies. Using these measurements, we recalibrate the $M_{\mathrm{sp}}$--$R_{\mathrm{sp}}$ scaling relation over a wide redshift range ($0.01 < z < 0.8$), finding a slope shallower than the constant-density expectation and no significant redshift evolution. We then apply this relation to \textsc{redMaPPer} clusters in the SDSS Northern Galactic Cap to derive splashback masses for more than $1.5\times10^4$ systems and construct the first observational splashback mass function based solely on photometric data. The resulting mass function agrees with simulation-based predictions at the high-mass end, while deviations at lower masses are consistent with known completeness limits of optical cluster catalogs. Our results demonstrate that splashback-based cluster sizes, masses, and abundances can be robustly measured in photometric surveys, enabling cosmological studies without spectroscopic or lensing data.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a fully photometric framework to measure individual galaxy cluster splashback radii and masses, constructing the first observational splashback mass function using SDSS data. Results show R_sp/R_200m ~ 1.1, a shallower M_sp-R_sp slope than constant-density expectation, and mass function agreement with simulations at high masses, enabling cosmological studies without spectroscopy or lensing.
AI.motivation: To develop a photometric-only method for measuring splashback radii and masses of individual clusters, avoiding the need for spectroscopic or weak-lensing data, and to construct the first observational splashback mass function for cosmological applications.
AI.method: A probabilistic cluster membership method using radial and photometric redshift information with an adaptive probability cut; applied to 499 clusters (CoMaLit) and over 15,000 redMaPPer clusters; cumulative galaxy number profiles modeled to recover splashback radii; M_sp-R_sp scaling relation recalibrated.
AI.result: Median R_sp/R_200m ~ 1.1; M_sp-R_sp slope shallower than constant-density expectation; no significant redshift evolution (0.01<z<0.8); splashback mass function matches simulations at high-mass end, with deviations at lower masses consistent with optical catalog completeness limits.
AI.conclusion: Splashback-based cluster sizes, masses, and abundances can be robustly measured with photometric data alone, enabling cosmological studies without spectroscopic or lensing observations.

title: Inferring Globular Cluster Initial Mass Function from Stellar Streams
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: The Gaia mission has provided precise astrometry and spectrophotometry for billions of stars in the Milky Way, enabling the identification and kinematic characterization of stellar streams. These streams, remnants of disrupted globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, have revealed the structure of the Milky Way's dark matter halo. We show that stellar streams also encode information about the initial mass function of globular clusters. We combine cold dark matter simulations that model the evolution and disruption of embedded globular clusters with observations of stellar streams and globular clusters to infer the initial cluster mass function. We find that initially more massive clusters produce more massive streams, but deposit a smaller fraction of their initial mass into those streams. Using stream mass and angular momentum measurements, we recover a declining, power-law-like initial mass function with a slope $α= 1.3\pm0.05$ for streams $\gtrsim 1000\,M_{\odot}$. This work establishes stellar streams as a novel probe of the early mass distribution of globular clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper uses stellar streams detected by Gaia, combined with cold dark matter simulations, to infer the initial mass function of globular clusters, finding a power-law slope of α = 1.3 ± 0.05 for streams ≳ 1000 M⊙.
AI.motivation: Stellar streams have previously been used to trace the Milky Way's dark matter halo structure. This work extends their utility to also probe the initial mass function of globular clusters, a fundamental property of early cluster formation.
AI.method: Cold dark matter simulations modeling the evolution and disruption of embedded globular clusters are combined with observational data of stellar streams and globular clusters to infer the initial cluster mass function.
AI.result: Initially more massive clusters produce more massive streams but deposit a smaller fraction of their initial mass into those streams. The inferred initial mass function is a declining power law with slope α = 1.3 ± 0.05 for streams ≳ 1000 M⊙.
AI.conclusion: Stellar streams are established as a novel probe of the early mass distribution of globular clusters, complementing traditional methods for studying cluster formation history.

title: Probing late-time deviations from $Λ$CDM with a quadratic dark energy expansion
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures
summary: We investigate the observational viability of a quadratic dark energy expansion (QDEE) model as a phenomenological extension of the standard $Λ\mathrm{CDM}$ cosmological framework. This approach introduces the additional degrees of freedom that permit mild late-time deviations from a constant dark-energy component while preserving the standard early-Universe behavior. We constrain the model using a comprehensive combination of cosmological datasets, including Planck 2018 cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements, Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) Data Release 6 (DR6) and South Pole Telescope (SPT-3G) data, Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2 (DR2), and the Pantheon Plus type Ia supernova compilation. Our results show that the QDEE framework shifts the inferred Hubble constant toward higher values relative to $Λ\mathrm{CDM}$, partially alleviating the tension with local measurements while remaining consistent with early-Universe constraints. Bayesian model comparison indicates strong evidence in favor of this framework over standard $Λ\mathrm{CDM}$ across multiple dataset combinations. Posterior predictive checks further demonstrate that the model yields predictions consistent with the observed data within statistical uncertainties.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a quadratic dark energy expansion (QDEE) model as an extension of ΛCDM, finding it alleviates the Hubble tension and is favored over ΛCDM in Bayesian model comparison across multiple cosmological datasets.
AI.motivation: To explore whether a phenomenological quadratic dark energy expansion model can observationally address tensions in the standard ΛCDM framework, particularly the Hubble constant discrepancy between early- and late-Universe measurements.
AI.method: The QDEE model is constrained using a comprehensive combination of datasets: Planck 2018 CMB, ACT DR6, SPT-3G, DESI DR2, and Pantheon Plus supernova data. Bayesian model comparison and posterior predictive checks are employed for validation.
AI.result: The QDEE model shifts H₀ toward higher values, partially alleviating the Hubble tension. Bayesian model comparison shows strong evidence favoring QDEE over ΛCDM across multiple dataset combinations. Posterior predictive checks confirm consistency with observations.
AI.conclusion: The QDEE framework offers a viable phenomenological extension of ΛCDM that improves fit to current cosmological data and reduces the Hubble tension while remaining consistent with early-Universe constraints.

title: Reconstruction of Reionization Histories from 21 cm Power-Spectrum Evolution with Artificial Neural Networks
comment: 22 pages. Submitted to Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics (RAA)
summary: We investigate whether the redshift evolution of the fixed-$k$ dimensionless 21 cm power spectrum, $Δ^2_{21}(k, z)$, contains sufficient information to reconstruct reionization histories $x_{\mathrm{HI}}(z)$ with artificial neural networks. Using semi-numerical realizations generated within a restricted three-parameter 21cmFAST model family, we train a compact feed-forward network to learn the inverse mapping from power-spectrum trajectories to the neutral-fraction history over $6 \le z \le 15$. For $k = 0.1$, $0.5$, and $1.0\ h\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, representative tests on an independent test set show that the midpoint redshift $z_{50}$ is recovered more accurately than the duration $Δz = z_{75} - z_{25}$: $z_{50}$ is reconstructed with MAE = 0.0046 and RMSE = 0.0100, whereas $Δz$ yields MAE = 0.0302 and RMSE = 0.0378. This result indicates that fixed-$k$ power-spectrum evolution carries stronger information about the timing of reionization than about the detailed width of the transition within the adopted prior. We further test an idealized foreground-free SKA1-Low-like thermal-plus-sample-variance noise model and find that the reconstruction remains stable in the favorable signal-to-noise regime considered here. These results demonstrate that neural networks can serve as prior-dependent inverse mapping for reconstructing reionization histories from 21 cm power-spectrum evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether fixed-k 21 cm power spectrum evolution can be used with neural networks to reconstruct reionization histories (neutral fraction x_HI(z)). Using 21cmFAST simulations, they train a feed-forward network and find that the midpoint redshift z_50 is accurately recovered (MAE=0.0046), while the duration Δz is less precise (MAE=0.0302). The method remains stable under SKA1-Low-like noise, demonstrating neural networks as promising prior-dependent inverse mappers for reionization history reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the redshift evolution of the dimensionless 21 cm power spectrum at fixed k contains sufficient information to reconstruct reionization histories using artificial neural networks, providing a data-driven inverse mapping approach.
AI.method: Semi-numerical 21cmFAST simulations within a restricted three-parameter model are used to generate training data. A compact feed-forward neural network learns the inverse mapping from power-spectrum trajectories (at k = 0.1, 0.5, 1.0 h Mpc^-1) to neutral-fraction history x_HI(z) over 6 ≤ z ≤ 15. Reconstruction is tested both without and with an idealized SKA1-Low-like noise model.
AI.result: z_50 (midpoint redshift) is recovered with MAE=0.0046 and RMSE=0.0100; Δz (duration, z_75 - z_25) yields MAE=0.0302 and RMSE=0.0378. Reconstruction remains stable under foreground-free SKA1-Low-like thermal-plus-sample-variance noise.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-k power-spectrum evolution carries stronger information about the timing of reionization (z_50) than the width (Δz). Neural networks can serve as prior-dependent inverse mapping tools for reconstructing reionization histories from 21 cm power-spectrum evolution.

title: On the correlation between globular clusters and the distribution of dark matter in galaxy clusters: the case of Abell 2744
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures - scripts available here: https://github.com/mreinacampos/starclusters-in-jwst/tree/a3df64fa8a821ece9ebc014b7010066971a07958/code_poisson_comparison/abell2744 - submitted to ApJ, comments welcome!
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) lie scattered around the inner $40\%$ of the virial radius of galaxy clusters, potentially being excellent tracers of the underlying mass distribution. In this paper, we present a statistical method based on assuming that the location of GCs around a galaxy cluster follows an inhomogenous spatial Poisson point process, and we use this method to assess to which galactic component GCs are better tracers of. We apply the method to the galaxy cluster Abell 2744, and we find that the spatial distribution of bright GCs roughly traces the three main interacting clumps in the galaxy cluster, alongside other galaxies with sizeable GC populations. The GC populations are more closely correlated to the predicted mass maps than any other galactic component (Spearman rank coefficients $>0.7$). A perk of this statistical method is that it allows us to distinguish to which map the agreement is closest to. In particular, we find that the Bright Blue GCs are compatible with the mass map solely derived from weak lensing, suggesting that they can provide complementary and independent information on the mass distribution in galaxy clusters with a similar level of detail to that of weak lensing. This statistical method is available in a public repository, and combined with catalogs of GCs in galaxy clusters at different cosmic epochs, it provides an independent method for investigating the mass distribution in these galactic environments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a statistical method based on an inhomogeneous spatial Poisson point process to assess how well globular clusters (GCs) trace mass distribution in galaxy clusters. Applied to Abell 2744, bright GCs strongly correlate with predicted mass maps (Spearman >0.7), with bright blue GCs specifically aligning with weak-lensing mass maps, offering an independent probe of cluster mass distribution.
AI.motivation: Globular clusters lie within the inner 40% of the virial radius of galaxy clusters and may serve as excellent tracers of the underlying mass distribution, but a rigorous statistical framework to quantify this relationship was lacking.
AI.method: A statistical method assuming GC locations follow an inhomogeneous spatial Poisson point process; applied to the galaxy cluster Abell 2744 to compare GC spatial distributions against mass maps and other galactic components.
AI.result: Bright GCs trace the three main interacting clumps in Abell 2744 and correlate more closely with predicted mass maps than any other galactic component (Spearman rank coefficients >0.7). Bright Blue GCs are specifically compatible with the weak-lensing-derived mass map.
AI.conclusion: GCs, particularly bright blue ones, can provide complementary and independent information on mass distribution in galaxy clusters at a level of detail similar to weak lensing; the method is publicly available for application to GC catalogs at different cosmic epochs.

title: CosmoForge I: A unified framework for QML power spectrum estimation and pixel-based likelihood analysis
comment: Prepared for submission to A&A, 20 pages, 6 figures
summary: Optimal power spectrum estimation on the largest angular scales of the cosmic microwave background relies on the Quadratic Maximum Likelihood (QML) estimator. Existing public implementations, however, each address only a subset of the problem and none combine power spectrum estimation with a self-consistent pixel-space likelihood within a single framework. We present CosmoForge, a public Python framework that unifies QML power spectrum estimation and pixel-based Gaussian likelihood evaluation for spin-0 and spin-2 fields on the sphere, with general (non-diagonal) noise covariances. The framework is split into three installable packages: CosmoCore (infrastructure), QUBE (Fisher and QML estimation), and PICSLike (pixel-space likelihood). A common interface exposes two interchangeable computation bases $-$ a harmonic basis built on the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity and a direct pixel-space basis $-$ selecting whichever is cheaper for the configuration at hand. Exact algorithmic optimisations reduce the Fisher cost to $\mathcal{O}(\ell_{\rm max}^4)$ for arbitrary noise covariances, with Numba JIT compilation of the hot kernels and MPI parallelisation of the likelihood scan. CosmoForge reproduces the Planck low-$\ell$ Fortran reference implementation across both the QML and pixel-space likelihood pipelines, consistently with double-precision arithmetic. Native multipole binning and three output normalisations (deconvolved, decorrelated, window-convolved) are exposed through a single code path, and the same covariance infrastructure powers both QML estimation and likelihood evaluation. CosmoForge offers a general-purpose, modular, and validated tool for the optimal analysis of large-scale data on the sphere. It is publicly available, pip-installable, and extensible to non-CMB observables.

AI.tldr: CosmoForge is a public Python framework unifying Quadratic Maximum Likelihood power spectrum estimation and pixel-based Gaussian likelihood evaluation for spin-0 and spin-2 fields on the sphere with general noise covariances, offering two interchangeable computation bases, exact algorithmic optimizations (Fisher cost O(ℓ⁴_max)), Numba JIT compilation, MPI parallelization, and validation against Planck low-ℓ Fortran references.
AI.motivation: Existing public QML implementations address only subsets of the power spectrum estimation problem and none combine QML estimation with a self-consistent pixel-space likelihood within a single framework, motivating a unified, modular tool.
AI.method: The framework splits into three packages (CosmoCore, QUBE, PICSLike) with a common interface exposing two bases: a harmonic basis using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity and a direct pixel-space basis. Algorithmic optimizations reduce Fisher cost to O(ℓ⁴_max) for arbitrary noise covariances, with Numba JIT and MPI parallelization.
AI.result: CosmoForge reproduces the Planck low-ℓ Fortran reference implementation across both QML and pixel-space likelihood pipelines with double-precision arithmetic. It supports native multipole binning and three output normalizations through a single code path.
AI.conclusion: CosmoForge offers a general-purpose, modular, validated, pip-installable tool for optimal analysis of large-scale CMB data on the sphere, extensible to non-CMB observables.

title: Formation of intermediate-mass black holes in young massive clusters detected with JWST: analytic mass estimates
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshift, including the "Cosmic Gems" arc ($z \sim 10.2$) and the "Firefly Sparkle" ($z \sim 8.3$). With masses in the range of $10^5$~M$_\odot$-$10^7$M$_\odot$ and half-mass radii in the range from $\sim0.4$-$15$ pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models. While direct N-body simulations are unfeasible for such a large population and given the high masses in many of the clusters, we estimate the IMBH masses formed via runaway stellar collisions in these specific environments utilizing a Fokker-Planck model together with an analytical framework for runaway collisions and mass loss through winds, which has been validated against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters. We apply this model to a sample of massive high-redshift clusters observed with JWST. Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range of $\sim10^2$ M$_\odot$ {\bf up to $\sim4\times 10^3$ M$_\odot$,} implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level. The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters ($R_h \sim 1$ pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of $1600-2700 {\rm M}_\odot$. Low metallicity ($Z \lesssim 0.02 \, {\rm Z}_\odot$) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass against stellar winds. We further demonstrate that the efficiencies obtained here are consistent with expectations based on direct N-body simulations. Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds, capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: The paper estimates that dense, metal-poor star clusters observed by JWST at high redshift (z~8-10) can form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via runaway stellar collisions, yielding typical masses of ~10² to ~4×10³ M☉, with the most compact cluster ("Cosmic Gems") producing seeds of 1600-2700 M☉, which could grow into supermassive black holes in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered a population of extremely dense, compact stellar systems at high redshift (e.g., "Cosmic Gems" at z~10.2, "Firefly Sparkle" at z~8.3) that are promising candidates for forming intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models, motivating the need to quantify their IMBH production efficiency.
AI.method: The authors use a Fokker-Planck model combined with an analytical framework for runaway stellar collisions and mass loss through stellar winds, validated against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters, applied to a sample of massive high-redshift clusters observed with JWST.
AI.result: Typical IMBH masses range from ~10² M☉ up to ~4×10³ M☉, with formation efficiencies at the few percent level. The "Cosmic Gems" cluster (R_h~1 pc) produces black hole seeds of 1600-2700 M☉. Low metallicity (Z≲0.02 Z☉) is critical for retaining seed mass against stellar winds.
AI.conclusion: Dense, metal-poor high-redshift clusters observed by JWST are viable factories for heavy IMBH seeds, capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe.

title: Euclid preparation: Testing multi-field inflation with galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum
summary: Primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) is a powerful probe of the origin of cosmic structure. Stage-IV surveys like \Euclid will measure galaxy $2$- and $3$-point clustering at high signal-to-noise, whose exploitation requires robust joint analysis. We prepare for Euclid's spectroscopic sample by validating a redshift-space power-spectrum and bispectrum pipeline (one-loop $P_\ell$, tree-level $B_\ell$) on Euclid-like mocks from Abacus-PNG $N$-body simulations with Gaussian and local-PNG initial conditions, using a halo occupation distribution (HOD) tuned to Euclid Flagship 2. We stress-test analysis choices -- PNG-bias parametrisation, priors, and scale cuts -- and perform null tests without PNG. In a `prior-agnostic setup', detection of the dominant PNG term $\propto f_{\rm NL} \, b_φ$ in single redshift bins is difficult; nevertheless, the bispectrum provides constraints on other PNG combinations that partially lift degeneracies. We propose a physically motivated prior on $b_φ$ that yields unbiased $f_{\rm NL}$ while accounting for theory uncertainty, and determine scale cuts that give unbiased $Λ$CDM and $f_{\rm NL}$. With $V_{\rm eff}=16\,h^{-3}\,{\rm Gpc}^3$ across four snapshots ($0.8\le z\le1.7$), our likelihood analyses recover $<1σ$ bias in $f_{\rm NL}$ and $Λ$CDM. At fixed cuts, $B_\ell$ alone reduces $σ({f_{\rm NL}})$ by $\sim29$--$46\%$ relative to $P_\ell$, and joint power spectrum-bispectrum analysis tightens a further $\sim8$--$13\%$; the cumulative gain from $z=0.8$ to $1.7$ is $\sim2.3$ for the joint case. The bispectrum quadrupole is key. Our strongest results are at $z=1.7$: $1.9σ$ for $f_{\rm NL} \, b_φ$ (prior-agnostic) and $2.35σ$ for $f_{\rm NL}$ (prior-based). Joint analyses thus offer strong prospects for testing multi-field inflation, pending end-to-end validation in the full Euclid geometry with observational systematics.

AI.tldr: This paper validates a redshift-space power-spectrum and bispectrum pipeline for Euclid's spectroscopic sample, using Abacus-PNG N-body simulations with local-PNG initial conditions. The authors test analysis choices, find that bispectrum constraints improve f_NL detection by ~29-46% over power spectrum alone, and achieve up to 2.35σ detection of f_NL at z=1.7 with a physically motivated prior on the PNG bias parameter b_φ.
AI.motivation: Primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) is a powerful probe of the origin of cosmic structure, and Stage-IV surveys like Euclid require robust joint analysis of galaxy 2- and 3-point clustering at high signal-to-noise to exploit this probe.
AI.method: Validated a redshift-space P_ℓ (one-loop) and B_ℓ (tree-level) pipeline on Euclid-like mocks from Abacus-PNG N-body simulations with Gaussian and local-PNG initial conditions, using an HOD tuned to Euclid Flagship 2. Stress-tested PNG-bias parametrization, priors, and scale cuts, with null tests without PNG. Proposed a physically motivated prior on b_φ.
AI.result: With V_eff=16 h^{-3} Gpc^3 across four snapshots (0.8≤z≤1.7), likelihood analyses recover <1σ bias in f_NL and ΛCDM. B_ℓ alone reduces σ(f_NL) by ~29-46% relative to P_ℓ; joint P_ℓ+B_ℓ tightens a further ~8-13%. Cumulative gain from z=0.8 to 1.7 is ~2.3 for joint case. Best results at z=1.7: 1.9σ for f_NL b_φ (prior-agnostic) and 2.35σ for f_NL (prior-based).
AI.conclusion: Joint power spectrum-bispectrum analyses offer strong prospects for testing multi-field inflation, pending end-to-end validation in the full Euclid geometry with observational systematics.

title: Milky Way Mapper decoded abundances -- I. Shared disc enrichment patterns
comment: accepted MNRAS
summary: Elemental abundances in the Milky Way disc trace its star-formation and enrichment history, but predicting these abundances from theory is limited by uncertain nucleosynthetic yields and poorly constrained chemical evolution models. Large surveys provide many abundances that enable multi-dimensional insight. However, having so much data available complicates joint visualisation and physical interpretation. Here, we examine the element abundances of 70,057 red giant stars from the Milky Way Mapper survey ([Fe/H] $> -1$), using 16 elements (O,~Mg,~Al,~Si,~S,~K,~Ca,~Ti,~V, ~Cr, Mn,~Fe,~Co,~Ni,~Ce,~Nd). To tackle the challenges of joint-interpretation of these elements, we build a generative data-driven model, expressing each star's abundance vector as a linear combination of a few ($4$) latent nucleosynthetic patterns. These patterns are shared among the population but vary in fraction between stars. The model accurately generates the measured abundances, with $χ^2 < 3$ (5) for $\sim$ 80\% (95\%) of stars. Model failures, where stars' abundances are not generated by the latent basis reveal accreted material and the role of multiple channels of metal-poor disk enrichment. We associate the recovered patterns, which represent high-precision ($σ_P \sim 3$\%) nucleosynthetic channels, with specific enrichment sources; (early and late) core-collapse supernovae, supernovae Type Ia, and asymptotic giant branch stars. We subsequently explore how the dominance of enrichment channels varies across age, metallicity and spatial extent of the disk, and show that enrichment patterns tightly couple to orbital properties. Mean pattern fractions vary smoothly with enrichment, and change rapidly across the valley between the high- and low-$α$ sequences. Our results provide a framework for improving our understanding of Galactic evolution in the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes abundance patterns of 70,057 red giant stars from the Milky Way Mapper survey using 16 elements. It builds a generative data-driven model with 4 latent nucleosynthetic patterns representing different enrichment sources (core-collapse SNe, SN Ia, AGB stars). The model accurately reproduces abundances for ~80-95% of stars, and failures reveal accreted material and metal-poor disk enrichment channels. Pattern fractions vary with age, metallicity, and orbital properties.
AI.motivation: Elemental abundances in the Milky Way disc trace star-formation and enrichment history, but predictions are limited by uncertain nucleosynthetic yields and poorly constrained chemical evolution models. Large surveys provide multi-dimensional abundance data that complicates joint visualization and physical interpretation, necessitating a data-driven approach.
AI.method: A generative data-driven model that expresses each star's abundance vector as a linear combination of 4 latent nucleosynthetic patterns shared among the population but varying in fraction between stars. Applied to 70,057 red giant stars with 16 elements from the Milky Way Mapper survey.
AI.result: The model accurately generates measured abundances, with χ² < 3 for ~80% and χ² < 5 for ~95% of stars. Pattern fractions vary smoothly with enrichment and change rapidly across the valley between high- and low-α sequences. Model failures reveal accreted material and multiple metal-poor disk enrichment channels.
AI.conclusion: The recovered patterns correspond to specific enrichment sources (early/late core-collapse SNe, SN Ia, AGB stars). Enrichment patterns tightly couple to orbital properties and vary across age and metallicity. This framework improves understanding of Galactic chemical evolution in the Milky Way.

title: Negative neutrino mass or negative dark energy?
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, submitted to PRD
summary: Recent cosmological analyses based on DESI and CMB data have revealed a tension between the inferred sum of neutrino masses and the minimum value allowed by neutrino oscillation experiments, when assuming an underlying $Λ$CDM model of cosmology. In this work, we perform a systematic exploration of alternative dark energy models, including models that can supply a negative dark energy density capable of reproducing the cosmological effects of negative effective neutrino masses. We argue that dark energy models can alleviate the tension by modifying the cosmic expansion rate over a specific redshift range relevant for CMB lensing, while matching BAO distance measurements from DESI at lower redshifts. Among the models considered, we find that a sign-switching cosmological constant model, $Λ_\mathrm{s}$CDM, is uniquely capable of recovering positive neutrino masses by modifying the expansion history in this way. For the combination of DESI DR2 BAO, CMB, and DES-Dovekie supernova data, the constraint on the effective neutrino mass shifts from $\sum m_{ν,\mathrm{eff}}=-0.075^{+0.039}_{-0.053}$ eV (68%) for $Λ$CDM to $\sum m_{ν,\mathrm{eff}}=0.055\pm0.050$ eV (68%) for $Λ_\mathrm{s}$CDM, with a 95% lower bound on the dark energy transition redshift, $z_\dagger>2.4$. Although $Λ_\mathrm{s}$CDM does not have the strongest overall statistical support among the models considered, when the $\sum m_{ν,\mathrm{eff}}$ parameter is allowed to vary, our findings point toward a specific sign- and redshift-structured contribution to the late-time expansion history as a viable way to alleviate the neutrino mass tension.

AI.tldr: This paper explores alternative dark energy models, particularly a sign-switching cosmological constant model (ΛsCDM), to resolve the tension between DESI+CMB data (which prefer negative neutrino mass sums) and oscillation experiments (which require positive masses). ΛsCDM modifies the expansion history in a specific redshift range, recovering positive neutrino masses (∑mν,eff=0.055±0.050 eV) while matching BAO data, though it does not have the strongest overall statistical support.
AI.motivation: Recent DESI and CMB data show a tension: the inferred sum of neutrino masses is below the minimum allowed by oscillation experiments under ΛCDM, suggesting the need for modified expansion physics.
AI.method: Systematic exploration of alternative dark energy models, including those with negative energy density mimicking negative effective neutrino masses. Focus on a sign-switching cosmological constant (ΛsCDM) that alters the expansion rate over a specific redshift range relevant to CMB lensing while matching DESI BAO data.
AI.result: ΛsCDM shifts the neutrino mass constraint from ∑mν,eff = -0.075+0.039-0.053 eV (ΛCDM) to 0.055±0.050 eV (ΛsCDM), with a dark energy transition redshift z† > 2.4 (95% lower bound).
AI.conclusion: ΛsCDM uniquely recovers positive neutrino masses among models considered, though not the statistically strongest. A sign- and redshift-structured late-time expansion history is a viable way to alleviate the neutrino mass tension.

title: Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF): The Link Between Star Cluster Formation and Expansion Rates
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to Apj
summary: We introduce the Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF), an AMUSE-based framework designed to connect embedded star formation histories to the dynamical evolution of young stellar systems. We model star formation through the gradual formation of stars inside an evolving background potential, where the global gas evolution is extracted from realistic magneto-hydrodynamical (MHD) simulations. In this first work, we focus on the global evolution of the natal gas and its dynamical imprint on the stellar population. Across all explored MHD setups, we find that the gas continues to collapse while stars are forming, increasing both the central concentration and velocity scale of the embedded stellar population before gas expulsion. Using a controlled grid of direct $N$-body simulations, we show that this embedded evolution strongly regulates both the survival and later expansion of young stellar systems. In particular, gas contraction shortens the stellar crossing time prior to gas expulsion, making the same gas-removal timescale effectively more adiabatic for the stars. We find that the present-day expansion of stellar associations still preserves information about the embedded dynamical state reached during formation. The expansion rate is limited by the velocity scale reached before gas expulsion, while the efficiency with which this velocity field is transformed into expansion depends on the gas-expulsion timescale. Finally, we show that some commonly used expansion diagnostics can directly trace the physical expansion rate of young stellar systems when full kinematic information is available, opening the possibility of using stellar kinematics to constrain the dynamical conditions of embedded star formation.

AI.tldr: D-CAF connects embedded star formation to the dynamical evolution of young stellar systems, showing that gas contraction before expulsion regulates stellar system survival and expansion, with present-day kinematics preserving information about the embedded formation phase.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between star formation histories (gradual formation in evolving gas potentials) and the subsequent dynamical evolution of young stellar systems, by developing a framework that connects realistic MHD simulations of gas to N-body dynamics of stars.
AI.method: The Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF) based on AMUSE, combining MHD-simulated evolving gas potentials with direct N-body simulations of gradually forming stars; explores a grid of MHD setups and gas-expulsion timescales.
AI.result: Gas continues collapsing during star formation, increasing central concentration and velocity scale of the embedded population. Gas contraction shortens the stellar crossing time before expulsion, making gas removal more adiabatic. Present-day expansion preserves information about the embedded dynamical state; expansion rate is limited by pre-expulsion velocity scale and gas-expulsion timescale. Some kinematic diagnostics can directly trace physical expansion rates.
AI.conclusion: The embedded dynamical evolution during gas contraction strongly regulates the survival and expansion of young stellar systems. Observed stellar kinematics can be used to constrain the dynamical conditions under which star formation occurred, bridging formation models to observed cluster properties.

title: Velocityformer: Broken-Symmetry-Matched Equivariant Graph Transformers for Cosmological Velocity Reconstruction
summary: Precise measurement of the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect - a probe of the large-scale distribution of baryonic matter, a key observable for cosmological inference - requires accurate reconstruction of galaxy velocities from spectroscopic surveys. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of kSZ measurements scales directly with the correlation coefficient $r$ between reconstructed and true velocities. We introduce Velocityformer, an equivariant graph transformer architecture designed to match the specific symmetry of the observational data. While the underlying physics is equivariant with respect to translations and rotations, observational effects break this symmetry due to the preferred line-of-sight direction. Matching the model's inductive bias to the data's broken symmetry consistently improves performance across all model sizes and training volumes, with Velocityformer improving $r$ by 35% over the standard linear theory baseline and outperforming ML baselines at every data volume. By matching the model's inductive bias to the data and conditioning on the physics-based long-wavelength solution, Velocityformer is highly data-efficient, training to high accuracy on as few as 4 low-fidelity simulations, and generalises zero-shot across input geometry, cosmological parameters, and galaxy sample. On high-fidelity simulated galaxy catalogues, this yields a 30% improvement in $r$ over the physical baseline, directly translating to the same SNR gain on observational data.

AI.tldr: Velocityformer, an equivariant graph transformer that respects the broken rotational symmetry of observational data (due to line-of-sight effects), improves velocity reconstruction correlation by 35% over linear theory and 30% over physical baselines, is highly data-efficient (training on as few as 4 low-fidelity simulations), and generalizes zero-shot across geometry, cosmology, and galaxy samples, directly boosting kSZ signal-to-noise.
AI.motivation: Accurate galaxy velocity reconstruction is critical for kSZ measurements, and the SNR scales with the correlation coefficient between reconstructed and true velocities; existing methods fail to account for the broken rotational symmetry induced by observational line-of-sight effects.
AI.method: Velocityformer is an equivariant graph transformer whose inductive bias matches the broken symmetry (translational equivariance retained, rotational equivariance broken along the line-of-sight), conditioned on physics-based long-wavelength solutions.
AI.result: 35% improvement in correlation coefficient over linear theory; outperforms ML baselines at all data volumes; trains on as few as 4 low-fidelity simulations; 30% improvement over physical baseline on high-fidelity catalogues; zero-shot generalization across geometry, cosmology, and galaxy samples.
AI.conclusion: Matching model inductive bias to the data's broken symmetry yields substantial gains in velocity reconstruction accuracy and data efficiency, directly translating to improved kSZ measurement SNR.

title: The chemo-dynamical complexity of ω Centauri: different kinematics for different populations
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The origin of ω Centauri remains one of the key open problems in stellar dynamics and chemical evolution. Its large abundance spreads and multiple populations suggest a formation history more complex than that of a typical globular cluster. We investigate whether the chemical sub-populations identified in APOGEE DR17 also exhibit distinct spatial and kinematic signatures. We analyse a sample of APOGEE DR17 red-giant stars using a Gaussian Mixture Model in an eight-dimensional chemical-abundance space. The resulting chemical components are combined with Gaia proper motions and APOGEE line-of-sight velocities to derive intrinsic mean velocities and velocity dispersions in all three observable directions. We measure both global kinematic quantities and radial profiles for each chemically defined group, extending from the inner regions to ~ 4 half-light radii. The Gaussian Mixture Model identifies five chemical components, which, when examined through their radial cumulative distributions, naturally group into two broader families characterised by lower and higher aluminium enrichment. The two families differ significantly in their spatial and kinematic properties: the Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and exhibit stronger radial anisotropy than the Al-poor stars, which remain closer to isotropy over the radial range probed. Despite these significant differences, the two populations share a common rotation pattern. This work represents the first chemo-dynamical study of ω Cen linking detailed chemical tagging to internal kinematics from the inner regions to the cluster outskirts. A formation path involving both hierarchical assembly within a dwarf-galaxy potential and centrally concentrated, chemically enriched star formation offers a natural explanation for the observed chemo-dynamical complexity.

AI.tldr: Using APOGEE DR17 and Gaia data, this study identifies five chemical components in ω Centauri via GMM, which group into Al-poor and Al-rich families. The Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and radially anisotropic, while both populations share a common rotation pattern, supporting a complex formation scenario involving hierarchical assembly and chemically enriched star formation.
AI.motivation: The origin of ω Centauri remains a key open problem due to its large abundance spreads and multiple populations, suggesting a more complex formation history than typical globular clusters.
AI.method: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) in eight-dimensional chemical-abundance space on APOGEE DR17 red-giant stars; combined with Gaia proper motions and APOGEE line-of-sight velocities to derive intrinsic kinematics and radial profiles out to ~4 half-light radii.
AI.result: Five chemical components identified, grouping into two families (Al-rich and Al-poor). Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and show stronger radial anisotropy; both families share a common rotation pattern.
AI.conclusion: The observed chemo-dynamical complexity is best explained by a formation path involving hierarchical assembly within a dwarf-galaxy potential and centrally concentrated, chemically enriched star formation.

title: Spider-Webb: enhanced star formation in low-mass galaxies within the Spiderweb protocluster revealed by JWST Pa$β$ narrow-band imaging
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Understanding the role of the environment in galaxy evolution is key to revealing the physical processes that regulate galaxy growth. We study the star formation activity of \pab\ emitters (PBEs) in the Spiderweb protocluster at $z=2.16$ using \textit{James Webb Space Telescope}/NIRCam narrow-band imaging. To investigate the environmental dependence of star formation, we derive star formation rates (SFRs) from the \pab\ emission line and compare SFRs in the Spiderweb protocluster with those in the field. Our main finding is that low-mass PBEs ($M_\star < 10^9\,M_\odot$) in the Spiderweb protocluster exhibit an enhancement in star formation compared to their field counterparts. This excess persists even without applying dust-attenuation corrections, indicating that enhanced star formation in the protocluster is robust regardless of whether a dust correction is applied. In contrast, intermediate- and high-mass PBEs ($M_\star > 10^9\,M_\odot$) show no significant deviation from the field, revealing a strong mass dependence in the environmental effects on star formation. No clear spatial concentration toward the cluster core of starbursting low-mass galaxies within the protocluster is seen, suggesting that their enhancement is not restricted to the cluster core. We suggest that starbursts in low-mass galaxies are facilitated by environmental processes such as galaxy mergers/interactions, and/or efficient gas supply. While the enhancement at the low-mass end is consistent with trends reported for other protoclusters at similar redshifts, the behaviour of star formation at intermediate masses ($10^{9} < M_\star/M_\odot < 10^{10}$) is not uniform across protoclusters. Our \pab-based results in the Spiderweb protocluster indicate that star-formation enhancement at cosmic noon depends on both mass and the dynamical state of the protocluster.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCam narrow-band imaging of Paα emitters in the Spiderweb protocluster at z=2.16, we find that low-mass galaxies (M⋆ < 10⁹ M☉) show enhanced star formation compared to field counterparts, while intermediate- and high-mass galaxies show no significant difference. The enhancement is not spatially concentrated toward the cluster core, suggesting environmental processes like mergers or gas supply drive the effect.
AI.motivation: To understand how environment regulates galaxy growth by studying the star formation activity of Paα emitters in the Spiderweb protocluster at z=2.16.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam narrow-band imaging of Paα emission lines to derive SFRs; comparison of SFRs between protocluster and field galaxies across different stellar mass bins; spatial distribution analysis.
AI.result: Low-mass PBEs (M⋆ < 10⁹ M☉) in the protocluster show enhanced star formation compared to field; no significant difference for intermediate- and high-mass PBEs; no strong spatial concentration of starbursting low-mass galaxies toward the cluster core.
AI.conclusion: Star-formation enhancement at cosmic noon depends on both galaxy mass and the dynamical state of the protocluster. Low-mass galaxy starbursts are likely driven by environmental processes (mergers/interactions, efficient gas supply), while intermediate-mass behavior varies across protoclusters.

title: Detection of a dark matter subhalo in the strongly lensed system PJ011646
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present a strong lensing analysis of the system PJ011646 using high-resolution ($\sim$0.1 arcsec) Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) dust-continuum observations to test for the presence of dark matter substructures. The lens mass distribution is modelled with an elliptical power law and third- and fourth-order multipoles (PL+MP; $m=3,4$), plus external shear. The multipoles have amplitudes of $\simeq$1.5 per cent of the convergence, consistent with nearby early-type galaxies, and improve the fit by $Δ\ln Z = 52.1$ relative to a pure PL model. Using this best-fitting macromodel, we perform a grid-based subhalo search in the image plane, parametrising the perturber as a spherical NFW. A subhalo in two locations in the image plane improves the fit by $Δ\ln Z>10$. Both correspond to the same location in the source plane, so they are partially degenerate; follow-up analysis suggests that only one is physically real. This is a subhalo of mass $M_{200} = {2.78}_{-0.66}^{+0.43} \times 10^{10} \, M_\odot$ and concentration $c_{200} = 30_{-7}^{+5}$, detected at $\sim$5.8$σ$ significance (relative to the PL+MP). This concentration is consistent with that expected for a typical tidally stripped Navarro-Frenk-White subhalo. The enclosed projected mass is most tightly constrained within a radius of 2 kpc, where we infer $M_{\rm sub} = {3.57}_{-0.14}^{+0.16}\times 10^9 \, M_\odot$. From grid cells consistent with no detection ($Δ\ln Z < 10$), we derive limits on the minimum subhalo mass that could have been detected at $3σ$ significance, finding $M_{200} \approx 8 \times 10^{8} \, M_\odot$ in the most sensitive regions of the lensed arcs. This demonstrates that ALMA continuum imaging at sub-arcsecond resolution can probe dark matter substructure in a mass regime where cold and warm dark matter models predict different abundances of subhalos.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution ALMA observations of the strong lens system PJ011646, we detect a dark matter subhalo with mass $M_{200} = 2.78 \times 10^{10} \, M_\odot$ at $\sim$5.8$\sigma$ significance, demonstrating that ALMA continuum imaging can probe substructure in the mass regime distinguishing cold and warm dark matter.
AI.motivation: To test for the presence of dark matter substructures in the lens system PJ011646 using high-resolution ALMA dust-continuum observations, aiming to probe a mass regime where cold and warm dark matter models predict different subhalo abundances.
AI.method: The lens mass distribution is modelled with an elliptical power law plus third- and fourth-order multipoles (PL+MP; $m=3,4$) and external shear. A grid-based subhalo search is performed in the image plane, parametrising the perturber as a spherical NFW profile. Bayesian evidence ($\Delta\ln Z$) is used for model comparison.
AI.result: A subhalo with $M_{200} = {2.78}_{-0.66}^{+0.43} \times 10^{10} \, M_\odot$ and concentration $c_{200} = 30_{-7}^{+5}$ is detected at $\sim$5.8$\sigma$ significance relative to PL+MP. The enclosed mass within 2 kpc is $M_{\rm sub} = {3.57}_{-0.14}^{+0.16}\times 10^9 \, M_\odot$. Non-detection limits yield $M_{200} \approx 8 \times 10^{8} \, M_\odot$ in the most sensitive regions.
AI.conclusion: ALMA continuum imaging at sub-arcsecond resolution can effectively probe dark matter substructure in the mass regime where cold and warm dark matter models predict different subhalo abundances.

title: Connecting CGM enrichment with Lyman alpha emitters at 2.9 < z < 6.7
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present the results of a blind search for Lyman $α$ emitters (LAEs) in three deep archival $z\sim6$ quasar fields from VLT/MUSE using state-of-the-art detection algorithms. We explore their connection with absorbers-particularly C IV and Mg II-in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) from the E-XQR-30 survey. We detect 156 LAEs at $2.9<z<6.7$ with luminosities ranging from log $L[\text{ergs}^{-1}]=$ 41.3 to 43.2. We find 34 and 14 galaxy associations with C IV and Mg II absorption respectively at $3.4<z<5.8$ within a line of sight velocity window of $\pm1000~\text{km}^{-1}$ and impact parameter of $<250$ pkpc. These systems have a weak anti-correlation with respect to the absorber strength-impact parameter relation. No Mg II systems are found within the virial radii of any LAE while four C IV absorbers are located within the virial radii of an LAE suggesting that low ionisation gas has a lower covering fraction. The LAEs have mild overdensity ratios of 1.7 and 1.9 around C IV and Mg II respectively. The stellar mass upper limits of $\text{log}~M_*<10.7~\text{M}_\odot$ estimated using Keck/NIRC2 imaging indicate that a low-mass, faint population of galaxies pollutes the CGM with metals. This paper serves as a pilot analysis for the forthcoming REQUIEM survey, an ESO Large Program on high redshift deep quasar fields.

AI.tldr: A blind search for 156 LAEs at z~3-6.7 in three VLT/MUSE quasar fields reveals weak associations with C IV and Mg II absorbers in the CGM, suggesting low-mass, faint galaxies are responsible for metal enrichment. Serves as pilot for the REQUIEM survey.
AI.motivation: To investigate the connection between Lyman α emitters (LAEs) and metal absorbers (C IV and Mg II) in the circumgalactic medium at high redshift (z~3-6), and to understand which galaxy population pollutes the CGM with metals.
AI.method: Blind search for LAEs in three archival z~6 quasar fields from VLT/MUSE using advanced detection algorithms; cross-correlation with C IV and Mg II absorbers from the E-XQR-30 survey; stellar mass upper limits from Keck/NIRC2 imaging.
AI.result: 156 LAEs detected (z=2.9-6.7; log L=41.3-43.2 erg/s). 34 C IV and 14 Mg II associations found. Weak anti-correlation between absorber strength and impact parameter. No Mg II within virial radii; 4 C IV absorbers found within virial radii. Overdensity ratios ~1.7-1.9. Stellar mass upper limits log M*<10.7 Msun.
AI.conclusion: Low-mass, faint galaxies (rather than massive ones) are the primary metal polluters of the high-z CGM. Low-ionization gas has lower covering fraction than high-ionization gas. This work is a pilot for the REQUIEM ESO Large Program.

title: Revisiting the mass metallicity relation and the fundamental metallicity relation of dwarf galaxies at cosmic noon with NIRISS
comment: resubmitted after addressing the referee report
summary: We extend the stellar-mass gas-phase metallicity relation (MZR) at $z = 1.1-3.4$ down to the extremely low-mass regime using 183 galaxies with $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 6.3-10.2$, based on deep JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy from the NGDEEP program. The derived MZR is in excellent agreement with our previous result from 50 galaxies in the GLASS-JWST sample, underscoring the robustness and universality of this relation. Together, these datasets constitute the largest sample of dwarf galaxies yet obtained with NIRISS. The observed MZR slope, $β\simeq0.24\pm0.03$, remains constant across nearly four orders of magnitude in stellar mass. Analytical modeling of the metal-loading factor of outflows ($ζ_\textrm{out}$) indicates that, at $M_*\lesssim10^8M_\odot$, $ζ_\textrm{out}$ becomes progressively less dominant than the gas fraction ($μ_\textrm{gas}$) in regulating the MZR slope. Using this enlarged NIRISS sample, we further test the existence of the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR). We find no robust evidence for an additional SFR dependence beyond the MZR, nor any reduction in metallicity scatter when SFR is included. Examination of systematic uncertainties in \oh, $M_*$ and SFR suggests that the MZR slope ($β\sim0.22$) is robust, and that different assumptions about the strong-line calibrations or star-formation history (SFH) of the galaxies change the slope by less than 1-$σ$. At the current depth of the NIRISS data, evidence for an FMR among high-redshift dwarf galaxies remains inconclusive, highlighting the need for larger samples, and deeper observations.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the stellar mass-gas phase metallicity relation (MZR) at z=1.1-3.4 to extremely low masses (log M*/M⊙ = 6.3-10.2) using 183 galaxies from JWST/NIRISS NGDEEP data. The MZR slope β≈0.24±0.03 is constant across ~4 dex in mass. At M*≲10⁸ M⊙, the metal-loading factor of outflows becomes less dominant than gas fraction in regulating the MZR slope. No robust evidence for a fundamental metallicity relation (additional SFR dependence) is found; the MZR slope is robust to systematic uncertainties.
AI.motivation: To extend the stellar mass-gas phase metallicity relation (MZR) to the extremely low-mass regime at high redshift (z=1.1-3.4) using deep JWST/NIRISS spectroscopy, and to test the existence of the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) among high-redshift dwarf galaxies.
AI.method: Analyzed 183 galaxies (log M*/M⊙ = 6.3-10.2) from deep JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy (NGDEEP program). Combined with 50 galaxies from GLASS-JWST. Used analytical modeling of the metal-loading factor of outflows (ζ_out) and gas fraction (μ_gas). Tested FMR by examining SFR dependence and metallicity scatter. Assessed systematic uncertainties in O/H, M*, and SFR from strong-line calibrations and star-formation history assumptions.
AI.result: MZR slope β=0.24±0.03 is constant across ~4 dex in mass. At M*≲10⁸ M⊙, ζ_out becomes progressively less dominant than μ_gas in regulating the MZR slope. No robust evidence for FMR (no additional SFR dependence, no reduction in scatter when including SFR). MZR slope β~0.22 is robust to systematic uncertainties (changes <1σ under different calibrations/SFH assumptions).
AI.conclusion: The MZR extends robustly to the extremely low-mass regime at high redshift. The metal-loading factor of outflows transitions from dominant to subdominant relative to gas fraction at low masses. Evidence for an FMR among high-redshift dwarf galaxies remains inconclusive with current NIRISS data depth, motivating larger samples and deeper observations.

title: Evolution of compressed clouds formed by filament coalescence. I. Oblique collisions
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan (PASJ)
summary: Stars are thought to form predominantly within filamentary molecular clouds. Recent studies have suggested that active star formation, including the formation of stellar clusters and massive stars, occurs within so-called "hub" structures, where multiple filaments converge. Understanding the formation and evolution of such hub-filament systems is therefore essential for unveiling the physical processes responsible for cluster and massive star formation, although the full picture remains incomplete. To address this, we have focused on filament-filament collisions as a potential formation mechanism of the hubs. In this study, we investigate the fundamental evolutionary processes of oblique collisions between two magnetized filaments using three-dimensional ideal magnetohydrodynamical simulations. As a model of initial filaments, we consider two identical finite-length magnetized filaments, varying the collision angle between their long axes, the collision velocity, which is set perpendicular to the long axes, and the initial line mass. We find that as the collision angle decreases from orthogonal to parallel, the compressed cloud becomes more prone to gravitational collapse. In addition, the instability of the post-collision compressed cloud can be explained by its energy balance. Specifically, if the absolute value of the gravitational energy exceeds the sum of the kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies immediately after the collision, the cloud undergoes gravitational collapse. Conversely, if the gravitational energy is smaller, the cloud expands. In addition, we estimate the upper limit of the collision velocity that enables hub-filament formation and identify the collision conditions favorable for massive star formation.

AI.tldr: Using 3D ideal MHD simulations, the authors investigate oblique collisions between two magnetized filaments as a mechanism for forming hub-filament systems, finding that smaller collision angles favor gravitational collapse, and that the post-collision cloud's fate (collapse vs. expansion) is governed by the energy balance between gravitational energy and the sum of kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and evolution of hub-filament systems, which are thought to be essential sites for cluster and massive star formation, by investigating filament-filament collisions as a potential formation mechanism.
AI.method: Three-dimensional ideal magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of oblique collisions between two identical finite-length magnetized filaments, varying collision angle, collision velocity (perpendicular to long axes), and initial line mass.
AI.result: Smaller collision angles (closer to parallel) make the compressed cloud more prone to gravitational collapse; the instability is determined by energy balance — collapse occurs when gravitational energy exceeds the sum of kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies post-collision; an upper limit on collision velocity for hub-filament formation is estimated.
AI.conclusion: Filament-filament collisions can explain hub-filament formation, with specific collision conditions favoring massive star formation; the energy balance criterion provides a predictive framework for post-collision cloud evolution.

title: Robustness Analysis of USmorph: II. Optimizing Feature Extraction, Dimensionality Reduction, and Clustering for Unsupervised Galaxy Morphology Classification
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We conduct a systematic robustness analysis of the unsupervised machine learning module within the hybrid framework \texttt{USmorph}. This module automatically discovers morphological structures from large-scale galaxy images, forming the foundation of the complete classification workflow. We evaluate five pre-trained models for feature extraction and identify an ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet as the most effective for capturing discriminative morphological features. UMAP is chosen for dimensionality reduction due to its optimal balance between preserving high-dimensional structure and computational efficiency. To enhance clustering stability, we propose a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme, which significantly improves label consistency and cluster purity. We compare the convergence, scalability, and quality of five clustering algorithms, finding that the Bagging voting scheme has the best performance with the combination of K-means, Birch, and Agg. A bagging clustering number of $K=16$ is used to achieve the optimal balance between classification granularity and manual validation efficiency. Our tests show that: (1) the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) reveals clear, compact cluster boundaries in low-dimensional space with strong feature separability; (2) the morphology classification results align with galaxy evolution theory, showing physically plausible distributions of different types in parameter space. These results demonstrate the technical robustness and scientific credibility of \texttt{USmorph}, establishing it as a reliable method for automated morphological classification in future large-scale surveys such as the China Space Station Telescope (CSST) mission.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically analyzes the robustness of USmorph's unsupervised machine learning module for galaxy morphology classification, identifying optimal feature extractor (ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet), dimensionality reduction (UMAP), and a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme (best with K-means, Birch, Agg at K=16) that enhances clustering stability. Results show strong feature separability via t-SNE and physically plausible distributions aligned with galaxy evolution theory, establishing USmorph as reliable for CSST surveys.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate the robustness of the unsupervised ML module within the USmorph hybrid framework, ensuring reliable automated morphological classification for large-scale galaxy surveys like CSST.
AI.method: Evaluated five pre-trained models for feature extraction (AlexNet best); used UMAP for dimensionality reduction; proposed a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme; compared five clustering algorithms (K-means, Birch, Agg optimal combination); used K=16 bagging clusters; validated via t-SNE visualization and physical parameter space distributions.
AI.result: ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet most effective; UMAP optimal for dimensionality reduction; Bagging voting scheme significantly improves clustering stability; K=16 achieves optimal classification granularity vs. manual validation efficiency; t-SNE shows clear compact cluster boundaries; morphology results align with galaxy evolution theory.
AI.conclusion: USmorph demonstrates technical robustness and scientific credibility, establishing it as a reliable method for automated morphological classification in future large-scale surveys such as CSST.

title: The TNG50-SKIRT Atlas: Multi-wavelength nonparametric galaxy morphology
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Context: Galaxy morphology is a fundamental property to describe galaxy evolution. However, the observed morphology of a particular galaxy may depend on the observed wavelength. Aims: Our aim is to investigate the wavelength dependence and the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators. Methods: We use the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas, an atlas of synthetic UV to near-infrared (NIR) broadband images for a complete stellar-mass-selected sample of 1154 galaxies extracted from the TNG50 cosmological simulation at $z = 0$. For each image, we calculate four nonparametric morphology indicators using the StatMorph code. Results: We find that the known correlations between the stellar mass and the morphological parameters measured in the optical, together with the Gini-$M_{20}$, concentration-Gini, and concentration-$M_{20}$ planes, are fully consistent with observational data. However, nonparametric morphological indicators change significantly with wavelength and that this wavelength dependence is stronger for disc-dominated than for bulge-dominated galaxies. The wavelength dependence of the morphology of our simulated TNG50 galaxies is consistent with measurements of local galaxies from the SINGS survey. We demonstrate that the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators is modest across the full galaxy population but can be significant for individual galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study uses the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas to analyze how nonparametric morphology indicators vary with wavelength and dust attenuation, finding that these indicators are wavelength-dependent (especially for disc-dominated galaxies) and consistent with observational data, while dust effects are modest globally but significant for individual galaxies.
AI.motivation: Galaxy morphology is fundamental to understanding galaxy evolution, but observed morphology can depend on the observed wavelength. The authors aim to investigate this wavelength dependence and the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators.
AI.method: The TNG50-SKIRT Atlas provides synthetic UV to NIR broadband images for 1154 stellar-mass-selected galaxies from the TNG50 simulation at z=0. Four nonparametric morphology indicators are calculated per image using the StatMorph code.
AI.result: Stellar mass-morphology correlations and morphological planes (Gini-M20, concentration-Gini, concentration-M20) agree with observations. However, nonparametric indicators change significantly with wavelength, with stronger dependence for disc-dominated galaxies. Dust attenuation effects are modest across the population but can be significant for individual galaxies. Results are consistent with SINGS survey measurements.
AI.conclusion: Wavelength dependence of galaxy morphology is confirmed and quantified, with disc-dominated galaxies being more affected. Dust attenuation has a mild population-level impact but can strongly affect individual galaxy morphology measurements.

title: Difference Between Half-mass Radius and Half-light Radius of Galaxies at 0.2 $< z <$ 2.5 Revealed by JWST/NIRCam Data
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables; published in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Using JWST observations in CANDELS fields, we measure the half-light radius ($r_{\rm e,light}$) and half-mass radius ($r_{\rm e,mass}$) for 14,333 galaxies with stellar masses $M_* > 10^9 M_\odot$ at redshifts $0.2 < z < 2.5$. To investigate the difference between $r_{\rm e,light}$ and $r_{\rm e,mass}$, we find that $r_{\rm e,light}$ is larger than $r_{\rm e,mass}$ for both quiescent galaxies (QGs) and star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Moreover, the difference between these two radii is clearly correlated with galaxy stellar mass, $r_{\rm e,light}$, and the rest-frame $U - V$ color. When examining the evolution of the $r_{\rm e,mass}/r_{\rm e,light}$ ratio, we observe a significant increase for SFGs at $z > 1.7$. In contrast, no clear increase is observed for QGs at $z > 1$, though a slight decreasing trend is seen between $0.2 < z < 1.0$. By fitting a linear relationship between galaxy size and stellar mass, we find that the slope for $r_{\rm e,light}$ is $\sim$ 0.1 to 0.3 dex larger than that for $r_{\rm e,mass}$. In terms of galaxy size evolution at a fixed stellar mass, the $r_{\rm e,mass}$ of QGs increases by a factor of $\sim$ 3 to 5 from $z \sim 2.5$ to $z \sim 0.2$. In contrast, the $r_{\rm e,mass}$ of SFGs increases by a factor of approximately 2 over the same redshift range, with this growth trend closely following that of their $r_{\rm e,light}$. These results indicate that previous insights into galaxy evolution based on $r_{\rm e,light}$ remain valid when considering $r_{\rm e,mass}$, although the specific slopes show some variations.

AI.tldr: Using JWST CANDELS data for 14,333 galaxies (M* > 10^9 M⊙, 0.2 < z < 2.5), the study compares half-light radii (r_e,light) and half-mass radii (r_e,mass), finding r_e,light > r_e,mass for both quiescent and star-forming galaxies. The ratio r_e,mass/r_e,light correlates with mass, size, and color. SFGs show significant ratio increase at z > 1.7; QGs show a slight decrease at 0.2 < z < 1.0. The r_e,mass of QGs grows 3-5× from z~2.5 to 0.2, while SFGs grow ~2×, similar to their r_e,light evolution. Prior conclusions based on r_e,light remain broadly valid with slope differences.
AI.motivation: To investigate the difference between half-light and half-mass radii in galaxies across cosmic time, and to assess whether previous galaxy evolution insights based on light-based size measurements hold when using mass-based size measurements.
AI.method: JWST observations in CANDELS fields were used to measure half-light radius (r_e,light) and half-mass radius (r_e,mass) for 14,333 galaxies with M* > 10^9 M⊙ at 0.2 < z < 2.5. The ratio r_e,mass/r_e,light was analyzed against stellar mass, r_e,light, rest-frame U-V color, and redshift. Linear fits of size versus stellar mass and size evolution at fixed mass were performed for both quiescent and star-forming galaxies.
AI.result: r_e,light > r_e,mass for both QGs and SFGs. The r_e,mass/r_e,light ratio correlates with stellar mass, r_e,light, and U-V color. SFGs show a significant increase in this ratio at z > 1.7; QGs show no clear increase at z > 1 but a slight decrease at 0.2 < z < 1.0. The slope for r_e,light is ~0.1-0.3 dex steeper than for r_e,mass. At fixed mass, QG r_e,mass grows 3-5× from z~2.5 to 0.2; SFG r_e,mass grows ~2×, tracking r_e,light evolution.
AI.conclusion: Prior insights into galaxy evolution based on r_e,light remain valid when considering r_e,mass, though specific slopes show some variations.

title: Dawn of the Milky Way disk: Determination of when a rotationally supported disk appears and dating the spin-up of the disk
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Paper accepted by ApJLetters
